title: Chicken Yassa, One-Pot
author: Khady Mbow
desc: A spicy marinade that pulls double duty as the sauce — cider vinegar and lime, four hours minimum, then everything in one pot.
longDesc: The cleanest architecture of the documented yassas: the marinade becomes the sauce, strained so the solids and liquid can be used at different stages. Two large yellow onions thinly sliced, six garlic cloves, a carrot, a third of a cup each of cider vinegar and fresh lime juice, two tablespoons of ginger, a tablespoon of lime zest, a scotch bonnet, two teaspoons of cracked peppercorns, a teaspoon of cayenne and a bay leaf, over two pounds of bone-in chicken thighs and drumsticks for at least four hours. The chicken browns eight minutes a side, whole allspice toasts two minutes, and the sauce reduces twenty minutes until the liquid has almost completely evaporated and the onions are lightly caramelised.
ingredients: 2 tbsp peeled and finely chopped fresh ginger
1 scotch bonnet chile, stemmed, seeded and finely chopped
2 lb bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs and drumsticks
2 tbsp peanut or vegetable oil, plus more for brushing
equipment: Large heavy pot or Dutch oven
steps: Marinate the chicken with the onions, garlic, carrot, vinegar, lime juice, ginger, lime zest, scotch bonnet, peppercorns, cayenne, bay leaf and salt for at least 4 hours, tossing occasionally.
Strain the marinade, keeping the solids and the liquid separate.
Brown the chicken in batches over medium-high, until golden brown on both sides, about 8 minutes per side.
Toast the allspice berries until fragrant, about 2 minutes.
Add the marinade solids and cook until the onions have softened, about 5 minutes.
Return the chicken, add the reserved liquid, cover, and simmer until the chicken is tender and cooked through, about 30 minutes.
Reduce the sauce uncovered over medium-high until the liquid has almost completely evaporated and the onions are lightly caramelised, about 20 minutes.
Season, pour the sauce over the chicken, and serve warm with rice.
chefTips: Straining the marinade is the move that makes this work — the solids go in to soften and the liquid goes in to braise, so neither job is compromised.
Four hours is a minimum and the recipe's total time is nearly five, so plan the day around it rather than the hour.
Eight minutes a side is longer than most browning instructions and it is deliberate: skin-on chicken needs that long to render properly.
The allspice goes in dry, straight after the chicken comes out, and toasts for two minutes in the rendered fat. That is a distinctive step no other documented yassa has.
Until the liquid has almost completely evaporated — that is the endpoint of the sauce, and twenty minutes uncovered on medium-high is what it takes.
Carrot in the marinade is unusual among the yassas and it sweetens the finished sauce. Keep it thinly sliced so it melts.
A note on the source's own title: it calls the dish grilled, but the method as printed is pan-browned. Follow the method.
commonMistakes: Tipping the whole marinade in at once instead of straining it.
Browning for four minutes a side instead of eight.
Leaving the chicken in while the sauce reduces, which overcooks it.
Stopping the reduction while liquid remains.
sources: Adapted from 'Chicken Yassa', saveur.com. BYLINE EXACTLY AS PRINTED: 'Khady Mbow'. Published 31 August 2012; updated 12 August 2022. Yield as printed: 'Serves 4–6'. Time as printed: 4 hours 50 minutes. TWO-PASS — pass two returned the ingredient list verbatim and pass one corroborated it in paraphrase, with NO DISAGREEMENT. Note the publication's 2012 index page lists the same recipe under a different title, 'Grilled Chicken in Caramelized Onion Sauce (Yassa Poulet)'.
THE HEADNOTE, quoted: 'A spicy marinade pulls double duty as the sweet-tart sauce for this one-pot southern Senegalese dish.'

Ingredient list as printed: 2 large yellow onions, thinly sliced; 6 garlic cloves, finely chopped; 1 medium carrot, thinly sliced; 1/3 cup apple cider vinegar; 1/3 cup fresh lime juice; 2 Tbsp. peeled and finely chopped fresh ginger; 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest; 1 Scotch bonnet chile, stemmed, seeded, and finely chopped; 2 tsp. coarsely cracked black peppercorns; 1 tsp. cayenne pepper; 1 bay leaf; Kosher salt; 2 lb. bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs and drumsticks; 1 tsp. whole allspice berries; 2 Tbsp. peanut or vegetable oil, plus more for brushing; Cooked white rice, for serving.

Times and cues as printed, by step: 'for at least 4 hours'; step two carries no time or cue; 'until golden brown on both sides, about 8 minutes per side'; 'until fragrant, about 2 minutes'; 'until the onions have softened, about 5 minutes'; 'until the chicken is tender and cooked through, about 30 minutes'; and 'until the liquid has almost completely evaporated and the onions are lightly caramelized, about 20 minutes'.
A SOURCING NOTE: the METHOD SHAPE above is SINGLE-PASS, from pass one's paraphrase. The quantities and the quoted times and cues are TWO-PASS. That split is recorded rather than glossed.

AN INCONSISTENCY IN THE SOURCE, recorded as printed: the index title says 'Grilled' and the headnote says 'one-pot', but the method is pan-browned, not grilled. No correction is made; the method is followed.

THE DISAGREEMENT WITH THE OTHER YASSAS, recorded and not reconciled: this version's acid is cider vinegar plus lime, and it uses NO mustard and NO olives at all. The Olive printing at SEN015 uses lemon and red wine vinegar with Dijon and olives, and roasts the chicken separately in a 200C oven. The Lake Isle version at SEN013 grills first and uses lime, white vinegar, Dijon and olives. Three authors, three different acids, and mustard in two of three. None averaged.
The five servings above is the midpoint of the printed 'Serves 4–6'.
healthBenefits: Onions, garlic and ginger together supply a broad range of anti-inflammatory compounds.
Lime juice and zest are a good source of vitamin C and limonene.
Cider vinegar adds acidity without sodium.
culturalNote: Published under a Senegalese cook's own name in an American food magazine in 2012, this is one of the earliest well-specified yassas in English, and its double-duty marinade is the neatest statement of what the dish actually is — an acid-and-onion braise where nothing is wasted.
